A bequest is something — money, property, or a valued possession — that a person officially leaves to someone else through their will. A will is a legal document in which a person states what should happen to their belongings after they die. The bequest only transfers to the recipient after the giver has passed away. Until then, it is simply a written promise.

Think of it this way: imagine a woman named Eleanor. She owns a house, a collection of rare books, $80,000 in savings, and a diamond ring passed down through her family. Before she dies, she writes a will stating: "I leave the ring to my niece, the books to the public library, and $80,000 to my friend Thomas." Each of those things she has chosen to leave — the ring, the books, the money — is a bequest. Eleanor is the one making the bequests. Her niece, the library, and Thomas are each receiving one.

Three key roles appear in any bequest:

The testator is the person who writes the will and decides what to leave behind. They are the source of the bequest. (Historically, a woman was called a "testatrix," though in modern usage "testator" applies to everyone.)

The beneficiary (also called a legatee) is the person or organization receiving the bequest. A beneficiary can be anyone the testator chooses — a family member, a close friend, a charity, a university, a hospital, or any institution.

The executor is the trusted person appointed to carry out the instructions in the will, making sure each bequest reaches the right recipient.

Almost any asset of value can be the subject of a bequest: cash and bank balances, real estate (houses, land), personal belongings (jewelry, artwork, furniture, vehicles), financial investments (stocks, bonds), intellectual property rights (royalties from a book or song), and even sentimental objects with no market value, like a handwritten letter or a family photograph album.
The four main types of bequest

Not all bequests are structured the same way, and understanding the types helps you use and encounter the word accurately.

A specific bequest names one exact item. For example: "I leave my grandfather's pocket watch to my son, Daniel." Only that particular watch goes to Daniel — nothing else, and no substitution.

A general bequest specifies an amount of money or a quantity of something, without pointing to a particular source. For example: "I leave $30,000 to my friend Maria." The money can come from any part of the estate — the testator isn't saying which account or asset it must come from.

A residuary bequest (sometimes called a residual bequest) leaves whatever remains of the estate after all other bequests have been fulfilled, all debts have been paid, and all taxes and expenses have been settled. For example: "I leave the remainder of my estate to my daughter, Claire." This is essentially a "whatever is left over" bequest, and it is extremely common in wills. It acts as a safety net to ensure nothing in the estate goes unaddressed.

A conditional bequest comes with a condition that the beneficiary must meet in order to receive it. For example: "I leave my apartment to my nephew, provided he has completed his university degree by the age of 30." If the condition is not met, the bequest either passes to someone else or falls back into the general estate.

A charitable bequest is simply a bequest made to a nonprofit organization, charity, school, religious institution, museum, or similar body rather than to an individual. For example: "I leave $200,000 to the children's hospital." Charitable bequests are one of the most significant ways that organizations receive long-term funding.
How a bequest differs from similar words

You will often encounter words that seem close to "bequest." Here is how they differ:

Bequest vs. Gift: A gift is something given while the giver is still alive — directly and in person. A bequest is only given after the giver's death, through a will. Your grandmother slipping you cash on your birthday is a gift. The same grandmother leaving you money in her will is a bequest. The timing and the mechanism are completely different.

Bequest vs. Inheritance: Inheritance is the broader term. It refers to everything a person receives from someone who has died — whether through a will or through laws that determine who gets what when there is no will. A bequest is specifically what is written into a will. Every bequest is part of an inheritance, but not every inheritance involves a bequest — when someone dies without a will (called dying "intestate"), the law distributes their estate, and there are no bequests, only legal inheritance.

Bequest vs. Legacy: In everyday language these two words are used almost interchangeably, and that is largely fine. The subtle difference is that "legacy" has a second, broader meaning — the lasting impact or contribution a person leaves on the world (a scientist's "legacy of discovery," a leader's "political legacy"). In precise legal and formal writing, "bequest" is the sharper, more specific word for what is left in a will, while "legacy" can carry that wider, symbolic weight too.

Bequest vs. Devise: This is a mostly legal and historical distinction. In older legal language, "devise" referred specifically to real property left in a will (land, buildings), while "bequest" referred to personal property (money, jewelry, movable objects). In modern everyday usage, "bequest" is used for both, and you rarely need to make this distinction unless you are reading older legal texts or studying property law.
The moment a bequest becomes real

This is an important nuance: a bequest is only a written intention while the testator is alive. The testator can update their will at any time — changing who receives what, removing a beneficiary entirely, or altering the amounts. The bequest does not transfer and cannot be claimed until the testator dies.

After death, the will goes through a legal process called probate, in which a court verifies that the will is valid and officially oversees the distribution of the estate. Only once probate is complete does a bequest become fully effective and the recipient legally entitled to what was left to them. In some cases — for example, if the estate has large debts — there may not be enough assets to fulfill all bequests in full, and beneficiaries may receive less than the will intended.

• She made a generous bequest of $1 million to her alma mater.
  • The art museum received a bequest of forty paintings from a private collector.
  • He was astonished to learn that a distant relative had included him as the beneficiary of a bequest.
  • The charity relies heavily on bequests to sustain its long-term programs.
  • Her bequest was conditional on her nephew completing his medical degree.

A few natural pairings will help you recognize and use the word fluently:

"Make a bequest" means to write one into your will. "Leave a bequest" is a softer, more conversational way of saying the same thing. "Receive a bequest" means to be the beneficiary. "Charitable bequest" describes a bequest to a nonprofit. "Cash bequest" means the bequest is specifically money. "Bequest in a will" is often used when clarifying the formal context.

A bequest is a deliberate, legally recorded decision to leave something of value to a specific person or organization through a will, with the transfer taking effect only upon the giver's death. It is one of the most precise and formal ways a person can express care, generosity, or intent — not in the moment, but across time, as a final act that outlasts them.
